Title: Lightweight obstacle detection for unmanned mining trucks in open- pit mines
Text:
Lightweight obstacle detection for 
unmanned mining trucks in open-
pit mines
Guangwei Liu, Jian Lei, Zhiqing Guo, Senlin Chai & Chonghui Ren
This paper aims to solve the problem of the difficulty in balancing the model size and detection 
accuracy of the unmanned mining truck detection network in open-pit mines, as well as the problem 
that the existing model is not suitable for mining truck equipment. To address this problem, we 
proposed a lightweight vehicle detection algorithm model based on the improvement of YOLOv8. 
Through a series of innovative structural adjustments and optimization strategies, the model has 
achieved high accuracy and low complexity. This paper replaces the backbone network of YOLOv8s 
with the FasterNet_t0 (FN) network. This network has the advantages of simple structure and high 
lightweight, which effectively reduces the amount of calculation and parameters of the model. Then 
the feature extraction structure of the YOLOv8 neck is replaced with the BiFPN (Bi-directional Feature 
Pyramid Network) structure. By increasing cross-layer connections and removing nodes with low 
contribution to feature fusion, the fusion and utilization of features of different scales are optimized, 
the model performance is further improved, and the number of parameters and calculations are 
reduced. To make up for the possible loss of accuracy caused by lightweight improvements, this 
paper replaces the detection head with Dynamic Head. This design can introduce the self-attention 
mechanism from the three dimensions of scale, space, and task, significantly improving the detection 
accuracy of the model while avoiding the additional computational burden. In terms of loss function, 
this paper introduces a combination of SIoU loss and NWD (normalized Gaussian Wasserstein distance) 
loss. These two adjustments enable the model to cope with different scenarios more accurately, 
especially the detection effect of small target mining trucks is significantly improved. In addition, this 
paper also adopts the amplitude-based layer adaptive sparse pruning algorithm (LAMP) to further 
compress the model size while maintaining efficient detection performance. Through this pruning 
strategy, the model further reduces its dependence on computing resources while maintaining key 
performance. In the experimental part, a dataset of 3000 images was first constructed, and these 
images were preprocessed, including image enhancement, denoising, cropping, and scaling. The 
experimental environment was set up on the Autodl cloud server, using the PyTorch 2.5.1 framework 
and Python 3.10 environment. Through four sets of ablation experiments, we verified the specific 
impact of each improvement on the model performance. The experimental results show that the 
lightweight improvement strategy significantly improves the detection accuracy of the model, while 
greatly reducing the number of parameters and calculations of the model. Finally, we conducted a 
comprehensive comparative analysis of the improved YOLOv8s model with other popular algorithms 
and models. The results show that our model leads in detection accuracy with 76.9%, which is more 
than 10% higher than the performance of similar models. At the same time, compared with other 
models that achieve similar accuracy levels, our model is only about 20% of the size. These results fully 
prove that the improvement strategy we adopted is feasible and has obvious advantages in improving 
model efficiency.
Keywords  Open-pit coal mine, YOLOv8, Mining truck inspection, Lightweight, FasterNet, Normalized 
Gaussian Wasserstein distance

and production. However, the traditional open-pit mining enterprises are trapped in three major dilemmas: 
First, there are many security risks. The mine environment is already complicated and hidden crisis, collapse, 
explosion, car accident and other accident risks, resulting in frequent industrial accidents, employees ' life safety

is threatened at all times ; second, the production efficiency is worrying. Mine operation is highly dependent on 
manpower. Long-term and high-intensity work is easy to make workers tired. In addition, some workers lack 
professional skills. These factors overlap with each other, which greatly reduces the overall operation efficiency. 
Third, the operating costs are high. The harsh working conditions of the mine make the recruitment difficult to 
become the norm. In order to attract the labor force, the enterprise has to raise the salary, which undoubtedly 
greatly increases the cost expenditure. With the vigorous development of artificial intelligence technology, 
the mineral industry has ushered in a turning point, and more and more automation equipment has been 
introduced. While improving production efficiency, it also provides a strong guarantee for the safety of mine 
operations. Among them, unmanned driving technology has become one of the core elements of building a 
smart mine. In the unmanned driving system, target detection, as the ' eyes ' of intelligent driving, shoulders the 
important task of perceiving the surrounding environment. However, the reality is that the existing detection 
models are usually bulky, resulting in extremely high requirements for hardware resources during actual 
deployment and operation. This limits the application of the model in resource-constrained edge equipment, 
especially in unmanned mining truck detection systems in complex environments such as open-pit mines. The 
open-pit mine environment is complex, and the mining truck may be disturbed by bumps and bad weather 
during driving, resulting in extremely complex images captured by the sensor, frequent loss of small target 
pixels, and greatly increased difficulty in target detection. The existing detection models do not perform well 
in the detection accuracy of small targets and occluded targets, and it is difficult to meet the safety production 
requirements in complex mining scenarios. Since the detection system needs to operate stably on mobile devices 
with relatively limited computing resources, it is particularly important to design a lightweight model. However, 
lightweight may lead to a decrease in model accuracy. How to maintain or improve the detection accuracy 
while reducing the model size is a key issue. Due to the strong generalization ability of deep learning model, 
more and more scholars have applied it to perception tasks of different scales and different scenes. In 2014, 
Girshick applied CNN to target detection and proposed the regional neural network RCNN1, which was a major 
advancement in the field of computer vision. Since then, there have been many improvements based on RCNN, 
such as Fast RCNN and Faster RCNN2. These networks are important milestones in the development of target 
detection technology. YOLOv1 was proposed by Redmon in 20163. It turns the target detection task into a single 
regression problem, which can predict the class probability of the target in real-time and mark the bounding 
box. However, YOLO has problems such as low bounding box regression accuracy and poor detection effect 
for small targets. SSD is a detection algorithm that combines YOLO with Faster RCNN4. Unlike YOLO, SSD 
predicts the bounding box and category probability of the target at different levels of the convolutional neural 
network and has limitations in detecting small targets and targets that are too long and wide. YOLOv2-v8 has 
been launched since 20175–9. They have been widely adopted by the academic community and applied to many 
practical application scenarios. In 2021, Liu et al.10 developed a system for identifying unsafe behaviors in coal 
mines by integrating MobileNetV3 into the YOLOv3 framework. The system showed excellent performance. 
In 2023, B et al.11 used YOLOv5 to enhance the detection capability of small targets in the field of unmanned 
driving, and achieved significant improvement in detection performance without increasing the number of 
model parameters. In the same year, Ruan et al.12 introduced a dual attention mechanism of space and channel 
to optimize the feature extraction and fusion process, providing a new algorithm for road obstacle detection 
in open-pit mines. The following year, W et al.13 re-parameterized the structure of YOLOv8 to make it more 
suitable for unmanned driving scenarios, especially for the need for real-time detection of small targets on 
highways. Tian et al.14 combined YOLOv8 with LMIENet image enhancement technology, first improving the 
quality and repairing the information of the original image, and then applying YOLOv8 for accurate detection. 
To solve the real-time problem, Zhang et al.15 incorporated a weighted bidirectional feature pyramid structure 
into YOLOv8 and developed a real-time monitoring system for mine personnel equipment, which significantly 
improved the model’s efficiency in feature fusion16.
These continuous algorithm innovations and improvements have significantly promoted the advancement of 
unmanned mining truck perception technology. Because of the significant advantages of YOLOv8 in efficiency 
and lightweight, this paper decided to further optimize it based on YOLOv8 to achieve higher performance 
standards.
Lightweight detection model for unmanned mining trucks
In the field of target detection for unmanned mining trucks, current models face many challenges. Among 
them, the model size is too large, which leads to extremely high hardware resource requirements during actual 
deployment and operation, limiting the scope of the application; at the same time, the detection accuracy of small 
targets and occluded targets is poor, which makes it difficult to meet the safety production needs in complex 
mining scenarios. Therefore, this study proposes a lightweight model based on YOLOv8s to improve the overall 
detection capability of unmanned mining truck target detection. The overall structural framework of the model 
is shown in Fig. 1. The model has been improved in the following targeted ways:
	(1)	 To achieve the goal of compressing the model size and reducing the model depth, the original CSPDarkNet 
17network is abandoned and the FasterNet_t0 network is introduced instead. Compared with the former, 
the FasterNet_t0 network has the significant advantages of simple structure and high lightweight. This re­
placement operation reduces the complexity of the model and provides a basis for the subsequent construc­
tion of an efficient and streamlined unmanned mining truck target detection model.
	(2)	 At the neck of YOLOv8s, the original PAN-FPN feature extraction structure is replaced with the BiFPN 
structure. The BiFPN structure significantly optimizes the fusion and utilization of features of different 
scales by removing nodes that have a low contribution to feature fusion and increasing cross-layer con­
nections. This optimization not only simplifies the feature fusion process but also effectively reduces the

	(3)	 Since the lightweight improvement leads to a loss of model accuracy, the YOLO Head is replaced by the 
Dynamic Head. The Dynamic Head introduces the self-attention mechanism from the three dimensions of 
scale, space, and task, which promotes the close integration of the detection head and attention and avoids 
redundancy. As a result, the model detection accuracy is improved without adding any additional compu­

	(4)	 SIoU is introduced instead of CIoU to improve the performance of the model. On the other hand, consid­
ering the existence of small target unmanned mining trucks in actual tasks, the calculation of NWD loss is 
added to the regression loss calculation link. Through these two adjustments, the model can respond to dif­
ferent scenarios more accurately, especially the detection effect of small target mining trucks is significantly 
improved, and the overall performance of the model is comprehensively enhanced.
Improved YOLOv8s mining truck detection model
Reconstruction backbone feature extraction
In the original model construction of YOLOv8, CSPDarknet was selected as the backbone feature extraction 
network. This network reduces the amount of calculation to a certain extent by cross-stage local connections.

However, its inherent disadvantages are also obvious. Too many convolutional layers make the network structure 
complicated, and it is not adaptable to edge devices with limited computing resources.
At present, many researchers tend to integrate lightweight networks such as GhostNet18, MobileNet19, 
and ShuffleNet to improve the situation. They mainly extract features using depthwise separable convolution 
(DSC), ghost convolution (GhostConv), group shuffle convolution (GSConv), etc., thereby reducing the overall 
complexity of the model. However, these convolution methods often come with additional data processing 
processes such as connection, shuffling, and pooling, which undoubtedly lengthens the running time invisibly. 
Moreover, the frequent memory access phenomenon caused by deep convolution harms the real-time 
performance of the detection model and slows down the detection efficiency. In this regard, this paper proposes 
to introduce a lightweight FasterNet network structure in the YOLOv8 system. Verified by tests on multiple 
devices, such as CPU, ARM, and GPU, FasterNet shows significant advantages over other existing lightweight 
networks in terms of simple structure, fast detection rate, and high accuracy, providing strong support for the 
efficient application of YOLOv8 in more scenarios20.
As shown in Fig. 1, the improved YOLOv8s model incorporates the FasterNet_t0 model into its backbone. 
This FasterNet_t0 model covers three key modules: The embedding layer and Merging layer, which rely on 4 × 4 
convolution and 2 × 2 convolution to implement their functions, specifically, they can complete downsampling 
operations and expand the number of channels at the same time. Moreover, each module of the FasterNet 
Block module, which is the core feature extraction part, is composed of a partial convolution (PConv) and two 
subsequent point-wise convolutions (PWConv)21. These three form an inverted residual block, and its structure 
is shown in Fig. 2.
As shown in Fig. 3, PConv is a new convolution operation of FasterNet, which is significantly different from 
the traditional convolution method. When processing input features, various previous convolution methods will 
perform convolution operations on all channels one by one. PConv is different. It only performs conventional 
convolution on a part of the channels in the input features to extract key features, and the remaining channels 
are not processed for the time being. To ensure the continuity of memory access, the front-end or rear-end 
continuous channels are usually selected to represent the entire feature map. Thanks to this unique design, 
PConv can greatly reduce the number of parameters and calculations, while its feature extraction performance 
is still excellent. Take Formula 1 as an example. When CP is set to 1/4 of C, compared with conventional 
convolution, PConv’s FLOPs (Floating Point Operations) drop sharply to 1/16 of conventional convolution, 
which reduces resource consumption while ensuring the efficient operation of the model22, and makes an 
outstanding contribution to the overall performance improvement of the model.

other hand, it can fully tap the computing potential of the device, prompting an all-round improvement in 
detection speed, and providing a basis for optimizing the overall performance of the model.
Weighted bidirectional feature pyramid structure
First, In a complex mining environment, how to deal with multi-scale features is one of the difficulties in target 
detection. Unmanned mining trucks may be bumpy during driving, resulting in missing pixel information 
of small targets captured by sensors. To solve this problem, this paper introduces a lighter and more efficient 
weighted bidirectional feature pyramid network (BiFPN)24, as shown in Fig. 4b below.
The neck network of YOLOv8 continues the PANet structure of YOLOv5, as shown in Fig. 4a. In the PANet 
structure, the FPN block is very important. It uses a top-down approach to deliver high-level features to the 
lower layers layer by layer, so that the lower layers can be supplemented with sufficient semantic features, and 
then obtain features with both strong semantics and high resolution, which is extremely beneficial for small 
target detection. Correspondingly, the PAN block adopts a bottom-up path to deliver low-level information to 
the higher layers, so that the information contained in the lower layers can be fully mined and utilized, thereby 
achieving an efficient fusion of multi-scale features. However, this two-way feature fusion strategy also has 
disadvantages, which inevitably lead to an increase in the number of parameters and the amount of calculation. 
In addition, there are many nodes with only one input edge in the PANet structure. These nodes play a limited 
role in the feature fusion network but increase the overall parameter amount of the model, slowing down the 
model operation efficiency. Therefore, the bidirectional feature pyramid network (BiFPN) is introduced to 
reduce the number of parameters and achieve lightweight25.
BiFPN achieves weighted feature fusion through fast normalization, and its definition is shown in formula 
(2). The weight wi is limited to a non-negative value using the ReLU activation number, and ε is set to 0.001 
to ensure numerical stability. At the same time, because the Softmax operation is avoided, the training speed 
is greatly improved. Because of the characteristics of bidirectional cross-scale connection and fast normalized 
feature fusion, BiFPN is more suitable for the mining truck detection network in open-pit mines.

Design of dynamic detection head
Under the harsh conditions of open-pit mines, a variety of adverse climatic conditions can significantly interfere 
with the visual monitoring of sensors, making it difficult to identify and track target objects. Therefore, when

detecting mining trucks in actual tasks, the detection unit of the target recognition model needs to be equipped 
with three key skills: the ability to identify the size of the target, the ability to identify the spatial location of the 
target, and the ability to understand the task requirements. These capabilities enable the model to accurately 
identify and locate target objects of various sizes, different positions, and various shapes. To enhance the 
effectiveness of the detection unit, this paper proposes an innovative detection unit design, the Dynamic Head26, 
which can comprehensively realize the sensitivity to the target scale, spatial location, and task requirements.
To reduce the computational complexity of the model, the Dynamic Head avoids directly integrating the 
self-attention mechanism in the detection unit. Instead, it adopts a divide-and-conquer strategy27, decomposing 
the attention mechanism into three independent dimensions: scale, space, and task, and the attention modules 
of these dimensions are arranged sequentially, and each module focuses on processing the attention of one 
dimension. Specifically, the scale attention submodule focuses on learning the importance of different semantic 
levels, thereby strengthening the feature representation of the target at different scales. The spatial attention 
submodule focuses on identifying various position information of the target in space, allowing the model to 
adapt to spatial changes such as scaling and rotation of the target. The task attention submodule is responsible 
for guiding different feature channels in the model to complete specific tasks. The structural design of Dynamic 
Head, as shown in Fig. 5, aims to improve detection performance through modularization and specialization 
while controlling the complexity of the model.

In actual open-pit mine production, when monitoring small unmanned mining trucks, these vehicles may 
only occupy a few pixels in the image, so their presence is easily disturbed by complex backgrounds. Even a 
small positioning error can lead to a significant reduction in the intersection over union (IOU), which directly 
affects the accuracy of detection. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a regression loss algorithm that 
combines the SIoU loss and the NWD (normalized Gaussian Wasserstein distance) loss. This algorithm adds 
the consideration of the normalized Gaussian Wasserstein distance based on the SIoU loss. The SIoU loss itself 
already considers the shape and direction differences between the predicted box and the true box, while the 
addition of the NWD loss further enhances the recognition ability of small targets. Through this combination, 
the algorithm not only maintains the fast convergence characteristics but also performs well in improving the 
detection performance of small targets in the image, thereby significantly improving the overall accuracy of 
detection.

Model pruning
To further compress the improved YOLOv8s model and simplify the pruning process, this paper adopts Layer 
Adaptive Magnitude Pruning (LAMP). The significant advantage of this method is that it does not require 
complex hyperparameter tuning or a lot of experimental work. By calculating the LAMP score, the algorithm 
can directly guide the pruning process and outperforms many existing pruning techniques in terms of pruning 
effect.
Amplitude-based layer-adaptive sparse pruning
For a neural network with a depth of d, when the input is x, its output can be expressed as:
	
f(x; W (1:d)) = W (d)δ(W (d−1)δ(· · · W (2)δ(W (1)x) · · · ) 
(16)
Among them, δ represents the activation function used to introduce nonlinearity, W(i) represents the weight 
matrix of the i-th layer in the neural network, and W(1:d) represents the set of all weight matrices from the first 
layer to the d-th layer of the network.
Considering that reducing the distortion of model output caused by pruning can enhance the performance of 
the pruned model, when only one layer is pruned, the setting of the optimal pruning standard can be simplified 
to: minimize the difference in the L2 norm of the layer output before and after pruning. That is:
	
min∥W −MeW ∥2

which is used to indicate which weights should be retained and which should be pruned. The L0 norm of M, that

k. This means that the pruning mask matrix M will ensure that only k or fewer weights are non-zero, thereby 
achieving sparsification.

Due to the nonlinear nature of the activation function δ, Eq. (19) is difficult to solve exactly. Therefore, the 
pruning process can be performed systematically in three stages. First, the impact of pruning each connection 
in the network on the model output is evaluated, and an initial score is assigned to each connection accordingly. 
Next, based on the calculated scores, the connections that have the least impact on the model performance are 
identified and removed. Then, using the pruned model, the importance of the remaining connections is re-
evaluated and their scores are updated31. This process is repeated, with each cycle including re-evaluation and 
pruning steps, until the predetermined pruning target is reached or the model performance no longer degrades 
significantly. Through this iterative approach, the network structure can be gradually optimized while ensuring 
that the key functions of the model are retained32.

Since the weight dimensions of fully connected layers and convolutional layers are different, a unified approach is 
adopted: First, all weight tensors are reshaped into one-dimensional arrays. Then, these one-dimensional weight 
vectors are sorted according to the calculated LAMP scores. After sorting, pruning operations are performed 
according to the order of weight importance, and weights that have less impact on model performance are 
removed first. This approach ensures the consistency and effectiveness of the pruning process while simplifying 
the processing of weights between different layers.

As can be seen from formula (22), the LAMP score is used to evaluate the importance of each connection in the 
network relative to other remaining connections in the same layer. After calculating the LAMP score, we adopt a 
global pruning strategy to identify and prune those connections with the lowest scores, that is, the connections 
that have the least impact on model performance. This process continues until the sparsity of the entire network 
reaches our pre-set target.
Amplitude-based layer adaptive sparse pruning can be completed in five steps: the first step is to sum the 
squares of the weights of each layer in the network to obtain the energy value of each layer weight, and these 
energy values ​are sorted in ascending order. The second step is to assign a LAMP score to the weight vector of 
each layer according to the sorted weight energy value to quantify the relative importance of each weight vector 
in the layer. The third step is then to integrate the LAMP scores of all layers to form a global weight importance 
list and sort it. The fourth step is to set the weight corresponding to the smallest LAMP score to 0 in the pruning 
mask matrix according to the global sorting result and mark it as the pruning target. The fifth step is to update 
the weight matrix according to formula (20) until the set sparsity is reached.
Experimental results and analysis
Dataset and experimental settings
In the initial stage of constructing the data set, we first carried out the collection of image data, which includes 
two main channels : one is to obtain image resources from the network, and the other is to shoot directly in 
the open-pit mine. Through these two ways, we have collected 3000 pictures. In order to improve the quality 
and clarity of these images, we preprocess them, including image enhancement and noise reduction. The image 
enhancement uses the sharpening filtering method to improve the clarity of the image by enhancing the high-
frequency components in the image. This method can make the details in the image more prominent and help the 
model to better identify the target. Non-local mean denoising is used to reduce noise. Non-local mean denoising 
calculates the value of the current block by finding similar blocks in the image, so as to achieve denoising effect. 
This method can not only effectively remove noise, but also maintain the edge and texture information of the 
image, which is very helpful to improve the performance of the detection algorithm. Increasing the diversity of 
data sets through enhancement techniques helps the model to learn more robust features, thereby improving 
its adaptability in different environments. Reducing the noise in the image can improve the image quality and 
make the model easier to identify useful features, which is particularly important for improving the detection 
accuracy to ensure that the visual effect of the image is optimized. Figure 7 below shows some of the data 
after preprocessing. The preprocessing step helps to reduce the data redundancy during model training, thereby 
supporting the lightweight goal of the model. Image quality (noise reduction, enhancement) and ensuring the 
clarity of the target object in the image (cropping, scaling), the preprocessing steps help to improve the detection 
accuracy of the model and the model can learn the feature representation under different environmental 
conditions, thereby improving its adaptability in complex environments.

Evaluation indicators
When deploying a lightweight unmanned mining truck detection model to edge devices, we must balance the 
detection accuracy and complexity of the model. To comprehensively evaluate the performance of the model, 
we selected the following key indicators: mean average accuracy (mPA50), Parameters/106, and Model Size/
MB and floating point operations (FLOPs), as well as the number of model parameters. Mean average accuracy 
(mPA50) is a comprehensive indicator that evaluates the precision and recall of the model at different confidence 
thresholds, providing a comprehensive perspective on the model’s detection performance. Floating point 
operations (FLOPs) an indicator that measures the computational complexity of the model, which reflects the 
amount of computation required for the model to perform a forward propagation. In edge deployment, the 
number of FLOPs directly affects the operating efficiency and resource consumption of the model.
By comprehensively considering these indicators, we can ensure that the deployed model not only performs 
well in detection tasks but also runs efficiently on resource-constrained edge devices. The calculation formula

When evaluating model performance, precision (P) is a key metric that reflects the proportion of samples that 
are positive among all samples predicted as positive by the model. Here, true positives (TP) refer to the number 
of positive samples correctly identified by the model, while false positives (FP) refer to the number of negative 
samples that the model mistakenly identifies as positive. Recall (R) is another important metric that measures 
the ratio of the number of targets correctly identified by the model to the total number of actual targets. In 
this metric, true positives (TP) also refer to the number of positive samples correctly identified by the model, 
while false negatives (FN) refer to the number of samples that are positive but not correctly identified by the 
model. For multi-category object detection tasks, we use the average accuracy (Pave) to evaluate the overall 
performance of the model on all categories. In addition, floating-point operations (FLOPs) are an indicator of the 
computational complexity of the model, which indicates the total number of floating-point operations required 
by the model during a forward propagation process. The calculation of FLOPs includes the amount of operations 
of convolutional layers, pooling layers, and fully connected layers. Taking the maximum pooling layer as an 
example, assuming that the size of the input feature map is Hin × Win × Cin, the size of the pooling kernel is K × 
K, and the step size is S. The maximum pooling operation mainly involves comparison and selection operations, 
and its computational complexity is relatively small. In this case, the FLOPs of the maximum pooling layer can be 
approximated as Hin × Win × Cin, which provides us with a reference for evaluating the computational efficiency 
of the model. Through these indicators, we can comprehensively evaluate the deployment effect of the model on 
edge devices to ensure that it can still maintain efficient operation in resource-constrained environments.
Improved YOLOv8 mining card detection model experiment
To reduce the model size, this paper makes two major architectural adjustments. First, we replace the backbone 
network of the YOLOv8s model with FasterNet_t0 (FN for short), which is a lightweight network designed to 
improve efficiency. Then, we replace the neck feature extraction module of YOLOv8 with BiFPN (Bi-directional 
Feature Pyramid Network, BF for short), which is a structure that can enhance feature fusion and extraction 
efficiency. The following table shows the size comparison of the model:
As can be seen from Table 2, by using FasterNet_t0 as the backbone network of the model, more than 20% 
parameter reduction, reduced computational effort, and reduced model size were achieved. When we only 
replaced the neck network, although the reduction in parameters and model size exceeded 30%, the reduction in 
computational effort was not significant. However, when we combined the replacement of the backbone network 
and the neck network, we achieved more significant lightweight results: 56.5% fewer parameters, 37% fewer

Model performance experiment
After the lightweight adjustment of the model, although the volume is reduced, the accuracy of the model is also 
affected to a certain extent. To ensure the accuracy of the lightweight model, this study improves the detection 
head and loss function of the model. Specifically, the detection head is upgraded to a Dynamic Head, which 
can handle the target detection task more effectively. At the same time, the regression loss function adopts a 
combination of NWD Loss and SIoU Loss, which aims to improve the prediction accuracy of the model for the 
target position and size. To evaluate the specific impact of these improvements on the performance of the model, 
we conducted four sets of ablation experiments using a self-made unmanned mining truck dataset while keeping 
the experimental conditions consistent. The ablation experiments are shown in Table 3 below. The purpose of 
these experiments is to test the contribution of each improved part to the model performance separately, to 
verify whether our method can maintain or even improve the detection accuracy of the model while reducing 
the model volume. Through these experiments, we can more clearly understand the impact of each component 
on the final performance of the model. In the experiment, we made three key improvements to the model, 
marked as A, B, and C. A is the backbone network of the model is replaced with FasterNet_t0, and the feature 
extraction structure is upgraded to BiFPN. B is the detection head improved to Dynamic Head, which is a new 
design that can better meet the detection needs of different targets. C is the improvement of the loss function. 
We replace the original CIoU loss with the new loss function proposed in this paper. This improvement aims to 
improve the convergence speed and detection accuracy of the model during training.
From the comparison of model performance in Table 3, in Experiment 1 without any improvement, mPA50 
is 0.652, the number of parameters (Parameters/106) is 11.13, and FLOPs/G is 28.5. When only Experiment 2 
with A improvement is performed, mPA50 is increased to 0.673, the number of parameters is greatly reduced to 
4.84, and FLOPs/G is reduced to 17.9, indicating that A improvement effectively reduces the complexity of the 
model while improving the accuracy. In Experiment 3 with B improvement, mPA50 reaches 0.702, the number 
of parameters increases slightly to 5.39, and FLOPs/G increases to 18.7, indicating that B improvement further 
improves the accuracy without significantly increasing resource consumption. In Experiment 4, when all three 
improvements were implemented, mPA50 reached the highest value of 0.742, and the number of parameters and 
FLOPs/G were the same as in Experiment 3, which fully demonstrated the comprehensive effectiveness of the 
three improvements and was able to significantly improve the detection accuracy of the model while controlling 
the model resource consumption.
Model pruning experiment
To minimize the computing resource requirements of smart edge devices, this paper implements a layer-adaptive 
pruning strategy based on weight amplitude after model optimization. This strategy allows the model to further 
reduce its dependence on computing resources while maintaining key performance. To evaluate the impact of 
different pruning levels on model performance and select the most suitable pruning model for actual application 
scenarios, we conducted a detailed analysis and statistics of the model performance under various pruning 
ratios. This process ensures that we can identify the best pruning scheme that can maintain ideal detection 
performance while compressing the model size and reducing the computational load.
As shown in Fig. 8, the accuracy of the model is improved at a lower pruning rate, which indicates that the 
adopted pruning technique effectively identifies and removes unnecessary weights in the network, plays a role 
similar to regularization, and thus enhances the generalization ability of the model. However, when the pruning 
rate exceeds 0.5, the accuracy of the model begins to show a downward trend. In particular, when the pruning 
rate is further increased to more than 0.7, although the volume of the model is significantly reduced, this large-
scale pruning also harms the representation ability of the model, resulting in a sharp drop in accuracy.

for use in complex environments such as open-pit mines. Through the above analysis, it is feasible to integrate 
the improved YOLOv8s model into the real-time monitoring system of autonomous mining vehicles, and it has 
many advantages. Here are some key reasons.
Reasoning speed: According to the experimental results, the reasoning time of the improved model on 
Raspberry Pi 4B is about 431.2 ms, which means that the model can quickly process image data in real-time 
monitoring system and meet the real-time requirements.
Resource consumption: The number of parameters and FLOPs of the model are significantly reduced, 
which helps to reduce the demand for computing resources and makes the model more suitable for running on 
resource-constrained edge devices.
Multi-environment detection: The model shows good detection performance in different environments, 
which indicates that the model can adapt to the changing environmental conditions of the open-pit mine.
Robustness: The improved model can still maintain high detection accuracy in harsh environments, which is 
crucial to ensure the continuity and safety of mining operations.
High precision detection: The mAP50 of the model reaches 0.769, which indicates that the model has high 
accuracy in detecting mining vehicles and can reliably identify and track vehicles.
Modular design: The model can be integrated into an existing monitoring system as a separate module, 
working with other components such as sensors, data processing, and user interfaces.
Scalability: The lightweight design of the model makes it easy to expand and upgrade, and can be adjusted 
and optimized according to future needs.
Conclusion
Given the problem that the existing open-pit mine unmanned mining truck detection network is difficult to 
balance between model size and accuracy, and is not suitable for mining truck equipment, this paper proposes a 
lightweight mining truck detection algorithm based on the improved YOLOv8. Through the following key steps, 
we achieved the optimization of the model. First, we replaced the backbone feature extraction network and the 
neck feature fusion network of the model, which significantly reduced the computational requirements and 
the number of parameters of the model. Secondly, to compensate for the possible decrease in accuracy during 
the lightweight process, we improved the detection head and adjusted the regression loss function. Finally, 
through the model pruning technology, we further reduced the size of the model while maintaining efficient 
detection performance. Experimental results show that our lightweight improvement strategy has a significant 
positive impact on the application of unmanned mining truck detection networks on intelligent edge devices. 
The improved YOLOv8s model not only maintains high detection accuracy but also reduces the number of 
parameters and calculations, making the model more accurate and efficient in actual vehicle detection tasks.In 
order to further adapt to the needs of future applications, the following are some suggestions. It is considered to 
fuse the model with other sensor data such as lidar and thermal imaging to improve the detection performance 
in complex environments. Multi-sensor fusion can provide more comprehensive environmental perception 
and enhance the adaptability of the model to different environmental conditions. Continuously optimize the 
algorithm to improve the efficiency and accuracy of the model in dealing with multimodal data. More advanced 
feature fusion techniques are studied to enable the model to make better use of information from different 
sensors. Further research on model lightweight technologies, such as network architecture search ( NAS ), 
knowledge distillation, etc., to reduce the model ‘s demand for computing resources and make it more suitable 
for running on resource-constrained edge devices. By implementing these recommendations, we can ensure 
that the model remains competitive in future applications and maximizes its effectiveness in a multi-sensor
